reason: Rich multi-source verification confirms Alcyoneus as a record-breaking 16-million-light-year structure propelled by an unexpectedly average host galaxy.
story: In February 2022, astronomers examining data from Europe's LOFAR radio telescope network uncovered a structure that shattered cosmic records: Alcyoneus, a radio galaxy spanning an astounding 16 million light-years. Emitted by twin plasma jets moving near the speed of light, its gargantuan lobes stretch more than one hundred Milky Ways laid end-to-end. Even from three billion light-years away, Alcyoneus's radio footprint looms as large across Earth's sky as the full moon. Yet when researchers peered into its core, expecting a record-shattering monster black hole, they found a suspiciously ordinary elliptical galaxy. Its black hole and stellar mass are completely average for its class, and its star birth is nearly dead. Scientists suspect Alcyoneus ballooned to unprecedented scales simply because it resides in an unusually empty filament of the cosmic web, where ejected plasma met almost no resistance.
angle: The largest known galactic structure in the universe stretches over 100 Milky Ways wide, yet was blown out by an entirely ordinary, run-of-the-mill galaxy.

claims.claim: Alcyoneus was discovered by a team led by astronomer Martijn Oei at Leiden Observatory.
The discovery was made using data from the Low-Frequency Array (LOFAR) radio telescope network.
The discovery paper was submitted and reported in February 2022.
The research was accepted for publication in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.
Alcyoneus is located in the northern constellation of Lynx.
The galaxy lies approximately 3 to 3.5 billion light-years from Earth.
The radio lobes of Alcyoneus span at least 16 million light-years (around 5 megaparsecs) across.
At the time of its 2022 discovery, Alcyoneus was described as the largest known structure of galactic origin.
The span of Alcyoneus's radio structure is equivalent to over 100 Milky Way galaxies laid end-to-end.
In Earth's sky, the angular span of Alcyoneus's radio lobes covers roughly the same area as the Moon.
The galaxy was named after Alcyoneus, a mythological giant from Greek legend.
The lobes were created by two magnetized jet streams blasting material out at nearly the speed of light.
Researchers previously missed the giant structure because its diffuse radio lobes are extremely faint.
The central host galaxy is an ordinary, quiescent elliptical galaxy rather than an extreme supermassive anomaly.
The host galaxy has a stellar mass of approximately 240 billion solar masses.
The central supermassive black hole is estimated at roughly 390 to 400 million solar masses.
The host galaxy has a star formation rate of only 0.016 solar masses per year.
Alcyoneus resides embedded in a filament of the cosmic web.
Scientists hypothesize the lobes grew to such extreme dimensions because the surrounding medium has a lower density than normal.
In 2024, Alcyoneus was surpassed as the largest radio galaxy structure by Porphyrion.

disputed: Distance from Earth: S2, S3, S4, and S6 report roughly 3 billion light-years, whereas S1 and S7 give 3.5 billion light-years (1.1 gigaparsecs). Script should say 'over three billion light-years away.'
Relative size multiplier to the Milky Way: S2, S4, and S6 state it equals roughly 100 Milky Ways end-to-end, whereas S3 states 160 times. Script should say 'over one hundred Milky Ways in a row.'

Classification as 'largest galaxy': Popular coverage often described Alcyoneus as the largest galaxy, but astronomical sources clarify that the 16-million-light-year extent belongs to ejected radio lobes rather than the stellar body of the host galaxy itself.
